# How Google interprets robots.txt

Day 1, 15:10 · Google · coverage: slides, transcript

Audio recording from the first minutes of the talk to its end, including a robots.txt quiz; the speaker is not named in the recording. The unknown-line slide stays with this talk: the recording reads out its example and value, although the photo's time stamp falls a few minutes after the hand-over to Lightning session B.

## Claims

- **[Slide]** The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
  <br><sub>`D1-C079` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · Extended by [D1-C520](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C521](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C017](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.
  <br><sub>`D1-C080` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C519](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C527](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C531](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C533](D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, `DEV-SRV-10`, the glossary term *User-agent group*</sub>

- **[Docs]** When matching rules to a URL, Google uses the most specific rule by path length. If rules conflict, it uses the least restrictive one.
  > "In case of conflicting rules, including those with wildcards, Google uses the least restrictive rule."
  <br><sub>`D1-C081` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C520](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C208](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** In robots.txt, * matches zero or more of any character and $ marks the end of the URL.
  <br><sub>`D1-C082` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C521](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Under the example file, Googlebot may crawl /, /politics/eu-vote and /sports/live/, and is blocked from /?utm_source=x, /index.html, /politics (no trailing slash), /live/ and /sports/live-score. An 'allow: /$' rule does not cover the homepage with tracking parameters.
  <br><sub>`D1-C083` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
  <br><sub>`D1-C084` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C516](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C017](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C842](D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours and reads only the first 500 KiB of the file.
  <br><sub>`D1-C085` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D3-C613](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Extended by [D3-C614](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
  > "Google-Extended does not impact a site's inclusion in Google Search nor is it used as a ranking signal in Google Search."
  <br><sub>`D1-C086` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers) · Extended by [D1-C513](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C522](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C523](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C025](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C121](D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-11`, the glossary term *Google-Extended*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Googlebot ignores an unknown line, such as a Content-signal line, placed between two user-agent lines and joins both user agents into one group, so the rules that follow apply to both; in the slide's example both are blocked.
  <br><sub>`D1-C087` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C526](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-06`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Bing closes the robots.txt group at an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines, so in the slide's example bingbot ends up not blocked while Googlebot is; the slide warned that different crawlers behave differently.
  > "Unpredictability is never a good time."
  <br><sub>`D1-C123` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D1-C526](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-06`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Content-Signal lines are now common because a large CDN provider adds them to its managed robots.txt files. Never place any non-standard directive between user-agent lines; put it after a group's rules and test the file with each search engine's tools, such as Bing's robots.txt tester and Google's open-source robots.txt parser.
  <br><sub>`D1-C088` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · Used by `DEV-SRV-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The robots.txt talk pointed to the robots.txt file of thebestfriedchickenever.com to show why comments in robots.txt are useful; the live file is mostly a large ASCII-art drawing written as # comment lines, followed by a single user-agent group (checked 2026-10-04).
  <br><sub>`D1-C089` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Docs]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
  <br><sub>`D1-C140` · Google Search Console Help · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [robots.txt report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/6062598) · Extended by [D1-C528](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C530](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D3-C615](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's robots.txt talk recalled that robots.txt began in 1994, when bots were crashing servers: Martijn Koster proposed a text file in the root of a site with rules for how automated clients may access it.
  <br><sub>`D1-C510` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2019/07/rep-id)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said it already supported robots.txt when it started crawling in 1996 as a Stanford PhD project, and has supported it ever since.
  <br><sub>`D1-C511` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2019/07/rep-id)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Robots.txt is now an IETF standard, RFC 9309, supported by basically all major crawlers; Google said it follows it because it is the right thing to do: anyone who wants to opt out of crawling should be able to.
  <br><sub>`D1-C512` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Robots Refresher: Future-proof Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2025/03/robots-future), [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2019/07/rep-id) · Extends [D1-C329](D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Repeated by [D2-C050](D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, the glossary term *RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The standard's official name is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP). Google stressed that it was designed in 1994 only to control which automated clients may access what on a site, and has nothing to do with how the content is used.
  <br><sub>`D1-C513` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2019/07/rep-id), [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers) · Extends [D1-C086](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by the glossary term *RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Robots.txt is not a security measure: the file sits at a predictable public address, so anyone can read the paths it disallows. Protect a secret folder with authentication, or do not put it on the internet.
  <br><sub>`D1-C514` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Used by `DEV-SRV-11`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The robots.txt file always sits in the root of the host; it cannot be placed anywhere else.
  <br><sub>`D1-C515` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Used by `DEV-SRV-04`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Robots.txt was made extremely simple by design so that anyone could implement and understand it; it was extended as websites grew more complex, but it still has only three rules: user-agent (a named crawler, or * for every crawler), disallow and allow.
  <br><sub>`D1-C516` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Robots Refresher: Future-proof Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2025/03/robots-future) · Extends [D1-C084](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Everything on a site is implicitly allowed, so an allow rule is only needed to re-open a specific path inside a disallowed one.
  <br><sub>`D1-C517` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Comments in robots.txt start with #, and a line without the # that a parser cannot read is ignored anyway, because the standard requires parsers to skip lines they cannot parse, so it acts like a comment.
  <br><sub>`D1-C518` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, the glossary term *RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler.
  <br><sub>`D1-C519` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extends [D1-C080](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-10`, the glossary term *User-agent group*</sub>

- **[Stage]** In the talk's worked example, disallow /*/live/ blocks /science/live/ and /sports/live/, because * matches any number of characters, and an allow /science/live/ rule re-opens that one path.
  <br><sub>`D1-C520` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extends [D1-C079](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extends [D1-C081](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** To let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage, use user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$; the $ ends the match, so /$ means only the root path and /cats$ means exactly /cats.
  <br><sub>`D1-C521` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extends [D1-C079](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extends [D1-C082](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.
  <br><sub>`D1-C522` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers) · Extends [D1-C086](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Repeats [D1-C485](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Extended by [D2-C025](D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-11`, the glossary term *Google-Extended*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The 'first' needs care: OpenAI documented how to block its GPTBot crawler in robots.txt in August 2023, before Google announced Google-Extended on 28 September 2023. What Google-Extended added was a token that controls AI-training use of pages fetched by Google's existing crawlers, separately from Search; Apple later introduced a similar token, Applebot-Extended.
  <br><sub>`D1-C523` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · [An update on web publisher controls](https://blog.google/technology/ai/an-update-on-web-publisher-controls/), [How to spot OpenAI's crawler bot and stop it slurping sites for training data](https://www.theregister.com/2023/08/08/openai_scraping_software/) · Extends [D1-C086](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Other companies have similar 'extended' robots.txt tokens; Google named Apple's Applebot-Extended.
  <br><sub>`D1-C524` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D1-C487](D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google called robots.txt extremely forgiving: a typo in a path only blocks the wrong path, a typo in a rule name such as disallow makes Google ignore that line, and the rest of the file is still used.
  <br><sub>`D1-C525` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D1-C532](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The real trouble is an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines: while writing RFC 9309, Google asked people whether the first crawler should then inherit the rules that follow, and opinions split roughly 50-50 (how the talk said the question was settled is unclear in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D1-C526` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C087](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extends [D1-C123](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The talk's fix for giving one crawler both an extra rule and the rules of another group: simply add another group for that crawler. Google's spec combines all groups that name the same user agent into one.
  <br><sub>`D1-C527` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extends [D1-C080](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-10`, the glossary term *User-agent group*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.
  <br><sub>`D1-C528` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [robots.txt report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/6062598) · Extends [D1-C140](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D3-C667](D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, `DEV-SRV-06`, the glossary term *robots.txt report*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said the robots.txt report helps catch CDNs that update a site's robots.txt without the owner's knowledge, and hosts that cloak the robots.txt file, which happens more often than people think.
  <br><sub>`D1-C529` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SRV-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said the robots.txt report uses the parser Google open-sourced at github.com/google/robotstxt.
  <br><sub>`D1-C530` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C140](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by the glossary term *robots.txt report*</sub>

- **[Stage]** In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow.
  <br><sub>`D1-C531` · Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extends [D1-C080](D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.
